strengths: The paper addresses a highly relevant and limiting bottleneck in current neural weight processing frameworks (e.g., nf2vec), which are traditionally restricted to a single, predefined network architecture.
First framework to demonstrate successful generalization to unseen NeRF architectures (e.g., different MLP layers, hidden dimensions, and tri-plane grid configurations) at test time.

The insight that a reconstruction/rendering loss alone leads to distinct architecture-based clusters in the latent space is interesting. Proposing a contrastive objective (using SigLIP) to enforce architecture-invariance is a logical and effective solution.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation that covers latent space analysis (t-SNE), classification, and instance-level retrieval, outperforming or matching prior specialized methods even in single-architecture settings.
The manuscript is well-written, clearly structured, and features high-quality figures that make the overall concept and results easy to comprehend.
weaknesses: The title 'Embed Any NeRF' is somewhat of an overstatement. The experiments are limited to simple MLP and tri-planar NeRFs. State-of-the-art NeRFs heavily rely on hash grids (e.g., Instant-NGP) or other complex representations (like 3D Gaussian Splatting), which are not evaluated and would likely introduce significant scaling issues for Graph Meta-Networks.

The training efficiency of the proposed method is a notable concern. According to Appendix D, training either $L_R$ or $L_{R+C}$ took approximately two weeks on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU. This high computational cost hinders scalability to larger datasets or more complex scene representations.

The contrastive alignment loss ($L_C$) requires paired data, i.e., having the same 3D object fitted with multiple different NeRF architectures. In practice, obtaining such multi-architecture pairs for arbitrary datasets can be highly computationally expensive since it requires training multiple NeRF models per scene.

strengths: Highly novel and timely contribution: First framework to perform representation learning on NeRFs directly from their weights in an architecture-agnostic manner, allowing generalization to unseen architectures.
Methodological soundness: The integration of Graph Meta-Networks (GMNs) with a contrastive loss (SigLIP) is technically elegant and well-justified for alignment of heterogeneous weight spaces.

Insightful analysis: The paper clearly demonstrates (via t-SNE and empirical evaluation) why reconstruction/rendering losses alone fail to bridge the architectural gap, and how contrastive learning successfully aligns the latent spaces.

Robust evaluation: Evaluated on multiple downstream tasks (classification, class-level retrieval, and instance-level cross-architecture retrieval) showing strong performance, even outperforming specialized single-architecture baselines.
High clarity: The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, with clear, illustrative figures and detailed appendices that ensure reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to relatively small and simple NeRF models (3-layer MLPs and 32x32 tri-planes) trained on synthetic ShapeNet objects. Extending this to state-of-the-art models like Instant-NGP with hash grids remains a challenge.
High training complexity: Training times are quite long (~2 weeks on an RTX 3090 for $L_R$ and $L_{R+C}$), which could limit accessibility and scalability of the method.

Graph scaling analysis: There is limited discussion on the computational complexity and memory footprint of converting dense architectures (like high-resolution tri-planes or voxel grids) into parameter graphs.

strengths: Pioneering Concept: This is the first architecture-agnostic framework capable of learning representation spaces over neural radiance fields (NeRFs) with arbitrary and even unseen architectures.

Methodological Contribution: The integration of Graph Meta-Networks (GMNs) with contrastive learning (specifically SigLIP) is a principled way to align different parameterizations of the same underlying continuous 3D signals. The authors clearly demonstrate and visualize why a standard rendering loss alone fails to align different weight-space architectures.

Rigorous Generalization Evaluation: The paper evaluates generalization to unseen architectures (e.g., changes in the number of layers, hidden dimensions, tri-plane spatial resolution, and channel numbers). The performance remains robust, which strongly validates the graph-based meta-network approach.

Clarity and Presentation: The manuscript is exceptionally well-structured, clear, and easy to follow. Figures 1-3 provide excellent intuitive visualizations of the pipeline and the effect of the different loss components on the latent space structure.
weaknesses: Computational Complexity: The training time is quite high. As mentioned in Appendix D, training the model with rendering losses takes around 2 weeks on an NVIDIA RTX 3090. A detailed discussion on the scalability of GMNs (e.g., the number of nodes/edges in the parameter graphs and how message passing scales with weight size) would be beneficial.

Limited Scale of Evaluated Architectures: The evaluated architectures (MLP with 3 hidden layers of size 64; tri-plane of 32x32x16) are very small and toy-like compared to modern high-resolution NeRFs, Instant-NGP hash grids, or 3D Gaussian Splatting. This limits the immediate practical applicability to state-of-the-art representations.

Alignment vs. Discriminativeness Trade-off: In Table 1, when evaluating classification on BOTH under multi-architecture training, the rendering loss ($L_R$) alone outperforms $L_{R+C}$ and $L_C$ (93.5% vs 91.9% vs 86.2%). This suggests that enforcing architecture-invariance via contrastive learning comes at a cost to the discriminative capacity of the learned representations. The authors should elaborate more on this trade-off.

strengths: Pioneering work in architecture-agnostic weight-space representation learning for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs), allowing a single model to process MLPs, tri-planes, and multi-resolution hash tables.

Introduces a novel and memory-efficient parameter-graph representation specifically for multi-resolution hash tables, enabling weight-space learning on state-of-the-art NeRF formats (like Instant-NGP) for the first time.

Thoughtful identification and solution for the architecture-bias in latent space: the paper reveals that rendering loss alone causes models to cluster by network architecture, and resolves this by successfully integrating a contrastive SigLIP loss.
Extensive and rigorous experimental evaluation across 13 diverse architectures, including testing on unseen architectures and testing generalization to an entirely different dataset (Objaverse).
Well-written manuscript with clear, informative, and high-quality figures that explain the graph construction and latent space dynamics.
weaknesses: The training time is extremely high (~2 weeks on an RTX A6000 for $L_R$ and $L_{R+C}$), which may limit the reproducibility and broader exploration of this approach by the research community.

The absolute retrieval metrics (Table 6) are still relatively low (e.g., 27.2% Recall@10 for the ALL/ALL setting), showing that matching instances across completely different network parameterizations remains a challenging and open problem.
The evaluation is restricted to object-centric synthetic NeRF datasets (ShapeNet, Objaverse). How the method scales to complex, unbounded, or real-world scenes remains unaddressed.

strengths: Pioneering Architecture-Agnostic Framework: It introduces the first framework capable of processing diverse and unseen NeRF weight architectures, addressing a major limitation of prior works (like nf2vec) which were restricted to single fixed architectures.

Novel Graph Conversion for Hash Tables: The paper proposes a highly memory-efficient parameter graph representation for multi-resolution hash tables. This enables weight space representation learning on highly popular hash-grid-based representations (e.g., Instant-NGP style) for the first time.

Contrastive Latent Alignment: Integrating a contrastive objective (SigLIP) with the traditional rendering loss successfully resolves the issue of architectural clustering in the latent space, forcing the GMN to align embeddings based on semantic content rather than specific parameterization.

Thorough Evaluation: Experiments across 13 architectures and 3 families (MLP, Tri-planes, Hash tables) demonstrate robust performance in classification and retrieval, outperforming previous single-architecture baselines and showing strong generalization to unseen architectures and external datasets (Objaverse).
weaknesses: Scalability Concerns: The investigated NeRF architectures are extremely small (e.g., MLPs with hidden dim of 32/64, hash table size of 2^12). In typical real-world settings, NeRFs and Instant-NGPs use much larger networks and hash tables (e.g., table size 2^19). Since Graph Meta-Networks (GMNs) operate on node/edge features per weight, the parameter graph size and message-passing overhead would likely explode for standard-sized models.

High Training Time / Computational Cost: Training the joint model (L_R+C) takes about 2 weeks on a high-end NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU, which is highly computationally intensive and limits the practical utility and reproducibility of the method.

Lack of Ablation on Contrastive Objectives: While SigLIP is used and shown to be effective, there is no comparative analysis or discussion showing how it performs relative to standard contrastive formulations (such as standard CLIP-style InfoNCE).

strengths: Pioneering Heterogeneous Weight-Space Learning: The paper takes a significant step forward from previous weight-space representation learning methods (like nf2vec or Cardace et al.) by proposing the first framework capable of handling diverse and unseen NeRF architectures during training.

Novel Graph Representation for Hash Tables: The paper introduces a clever parameter graph conversion for multi-resolution hash tables. This representation avoids the cubic complexity of explicit voxel-grid modeling, preserving the memory efficiency of the hash table while allowing Graph Meta-Networks (GMNs) to process it.

Insightful Latent Space Analysis: The observation and t-SNE visualization showing that a pure rendering loss causes NeRFs to cluster by their network architecture rather than their 3D content is highly insightful. The integration of a contrastive loss is a logical and well-justified solution to this issue.

Thorough Architecture Evaluation: The authors evaluated their method across 13 different architectures belonging to three distinct families (MLPs, tri-planes, hash tables), including evaluating on architectures unseen during training.
weaknesses: Simplified NeRF Formulation (Lack of View Dependence): The NeRFs evaluated in this work are simplified to map (x, y, z) to (r, g, b, sigma) without any view-dependent effects (omitting the viewing direction). While this follows some previous works, it significantly deviates from standard NeRFs which use view-dependent color rendering. Restricting the models to view-independent representations limits the practical utility of this framework on standard, real-world NeRF datasets where specularities and view-dependent effects are crucial.

Very Long Training Times / Computational Efficiency: As noted in Appendix D, training the GMN with the joint rendering and contrastive loss takes approximately 2 weeks on an NVIDIA RTX A6000. This extremely long training time makes the method very expensive to train, scale, or reproduce, especially considering that the experiments are conducted on relatively small networks on synthetic ShapeNet objects. Scaling this up to larger, more modern NeRF models or larger datasets seems computationally prohibitive.

Low Absolute Cross-Architecture Retrieval Accuracy: While the contrastive loss drastically improves over the baseline rendering loss for instance retrieval, the absolute retrieval performance remains quite low. In Table 6, the overall Recall@1 for ALL/ALL is only 5.3%, and Recall@10 is 27.2%. Even for pairwise retrieval, any combination involving HASH exhibits low performance (e.g., HASH/TRI Recall@1 is 9.5%, HASH/MLP Recall@1 is 13.5%). This suggests that fully aligning diverse architectures—particularly those utilizing discrete, hashed spatial representations—remains a largely unsolved challenge, and the proposed alignment is weak.

Limited Dataset Diversity: The quantitative evaluation is restricted to the synthetic ShapeNetRender dataset. Real-world scenes (e.g., from ScanNet, LLFF, or Tanks and Temples) typically present much more complex geometry, lighting, and background noise. The generalization experiment on ObjaNeRF is purely qualitative. A more rigorous quantitative assessment on a more diverse or real-world dataset is needed to prove the robustness of the representation.

Heuristic Hyperparameter Tuning and Lack of Ablations: The choice of the loss blending weight is determined heuristically based on matching the magnitudes of the losses. There is a lack of ablation studies analyzing how sensitive the downstream performance is to this value. Furthermore, other contrastive loss formulations (such as standard InfoNCE/CLIP loss) are not compared against the selected SigLIP loss, leaving it unclear if SigLIP is indeed the optimal choice here.
